At first glance, a lantern grazer looks like a small grove of luminous trees walking through the fog.

It lives on Veyra, a rocky planet that always turns the same face toward its red sun. One hemisphere is scorched and dry; the other lies beneath permanent ice. Between them runs a narrow belt of twilight, where warm winds meet cold air and fill the valleys with mist. Here, among shallow mineral lakes, the lantern grazer moves slowly through forests of black, ribbon-shaped vegetation.

An adult stands about three meters tall, though most of that height comes from the branching structures growing from its back. Its body is low and broad, shaped like an overturned boat, and supported by six jointed legs. Each leg ends in a wide, flexible pad that spreads under the animal’s weight. When it crosses soft mud, the pads leave prints resembling open flowers.

Its skin is translucent gray. Beneath it, bundles of dark muscle contract around pale chambers filled with circulating fluid. Along its flanks, overlapping plates of silica form a flexible armor. Young grazers have nearly clear plates, but older individuals accumulate mineral stains: copper-green streaks, rusty freckles, and violet edges. A herd viewed through the mist resembles a procession of weathered stained-glass windows.

The “trees” on its back are hollow, branching fans covered in delicate amber membranes. These membranes shelter colonies of microscopic organisms that harvest the red sun’s faint light. In exchange for sugars, the grazer supplies its passengers with water and minerals drawn from the lake mud.

Light alone cannot sustain such a large animal. Beneath the front of its body hangs a muscular feeding ribbon, normally rolled into a tight spiral. When feeding, the grazer unfurls this ribbon and presses it against submerged stones. Thousands of tiny hooks scrape away the dense microbial films growing there. A grazing herd makes a soft, persistent sound like brushes moving over rough paper.

The lantern grazer has no recognizable face. Instead, a ring of sensory pits circles its forward end. Some detect warmth; others sample chemicals carried by wind or water. Two glossy patches distinguish light from shadow, but its most precise sense comes through its feet. Sensitive membranes in each sole detect vibrations passing through the ground.

A grazer can recognize the footsteps of its herd members long before they emerge from the fog.

It communicates by tapping its legs in patterns. Three quick taps may draw nearby animals toward a rich feeding patch. A slow, repeated stamp gathers wandering young. When danger approaches, the whole herd can become motionless almost simultaneously, warned by a signal transmitted through the mud.

Its name comes from the glow inside its branching fans. Normally, this light is faint—just enough to outline each amber membrane. When threatened by Veyra’s low-flying predators, however, the grazer pumps luminous fluid into the branches, producing a sudden blue-white flash. At the same time, it folds its legs and drops against the ground, protecting its soft underside. The predator is left striking at a dazzling thicket of brittle, replaceable branches.

Lantern grazers lay clusters of leathery eggs in warm mineral springs. Hatchlings are flat, dark creatures no larger than a human hand, with none of the adult’s luminous ornaments. For their first year, they shelter beneath an adult’s body, feeding on scraps loosened by its scraping ribbon.

Only when a young grazer develops its first branching fan does it begin walking beyond that shelter.

In Veyra’s endless dusk, these juveniles are easy to recognize: small gray shapes moving carefully between towering adults, each carrying a single trembling light.

### The Glassback of Nacre

At first glance, a glassback looks like a piece of the landscape that has decided to move.

It lives on Nacre, a cold planet circling a dim red star. Most of the surface is covered in shallow, salty water, interrupted by black volcanic ridges. Beneath the planet’s thick atmosphere, daylight is the color of a banked fire. Long tides creep across the flats, covering and uncovering the same kilometers of stone.

An adult glassback is about two meters long and no taller than a low table. Its body resembles a flattened teardrop, broad at the front and tapering into a flexible tail. Six jointed legs carry it over the mud. Each foot spreads into a fan of soft, fingerlike pads that can grip slick rock or distribute its weight over fragile crusts of salt.

Its most striking feature is its shell.

The shell is translucent, built from overlapping plates of a mineral-rich material similar to cloudy glass. Inside it runs a branching network of dark violet tissue. In daylight, these branches slowly spread and flatten, turning the glassback’s back into a living collector for the weak starlight.

The violet tissue belongs to colonies of microscopic organisms that live within the shell. They make nutrients from light and dissolved chemicals, sharing some with their host. In return, the glassback carries them between mineral-rich pools and shelters them from the cold. An animal deprived of its colonies can survive by scavenging, but it grows slowly and rarely reproduces.

Under the shell, its body is pale and muscular. Three dark digestive sacs contract visibly after a meal. When frightened, the animal draws an opaque fluid into channels beneath its armor, hiding its vulnerable organs behind a milky veil.

The glassback has no face in the familiar sense. Around its forward edge hangs a fringe of sensory tendrils, each tipped with a silver bead. These detect water movement, dissolved chemicals, and the faint electrical activity of nearby life. Two recessed pits distinguish light from darkness, but it recognizes most things through touch and chemistry.

It feeds by lowering its underside onto a patch of mud and extending a circular rasp. The rasp scrapes up microbial mats and soft, burrowing organisms, leaving pale rings on the dark ground. A feeding glassback makes a steady, delicate clicking sound, like someone turning a small mechanism beneath a blanket.

Although usually solitary, glassbacks gather before severe storms. They sense pressure changes through thin membranes inside their leg joints, sometimes hours before the wind rises. In sheltered hollows, they press their shells together and anchor their feet to the rock. A gathering may contain thirty animals, fitted into an uneven, glittering pavement. Warmth escaping from their bodies keeps the water between them from freezing.

Their young develop in shallow cups excavated near geothermal seeps. A parent deposits a cluster of leathery capsules, then rubs its shell against them, coating each with the violet organisms its offspring will need. For several weeks, it remains nearby, clearing sediment from the nest and driving scavengers away with blows of its tail.

Newly hatched glassbacks are almost transparent. Their legs seem too large for their bodies, and their shells bend when touched. Only after months of feeding do the plates harden and the first purple branches appear.

A glassback may live for more than a century. Old individuals can be recognized by their thick, scratched shells and the small forests of harmless filter-feeders growing along their backs. When one crosses a still pool, those tiny passengers open their feathery mouths into its wake.

Long after the animal has passed, a winding trail remains in the mud: six rows of footprints, a narrow tail groove, and occasional perfect circles where it stopped to eat.

### The Glass-Sailed Wanderer

On the planet Nacre, the sun never rises or sets. One hemisphere faces its small red star forever, while the other lies beneath an immense cap of ice. Between them runs a belt of perpetual twilight, where warm winds sweep across black stone plains and shallow, copper-colored lakes.

Here lives the glass-sailed wanderer.

An adult stands about as tall as a horse, but its body hangs low between six slender legs. Each leg ends in three spreading toes tipped with dark hooks, allowing it to grip the porous volcanic ground when the winds strengthen. Its skin is pale violet and faintly translucent. Beneath it, bundles of silvery muscle contract around a long digestive chamber, and slow pulses of blue fluid travel through branching vessels.

From a distance, the animal looks like a lantern walking inside a sheet of crumpled glass.

The “glass” is a flexible sail that rises from its back. Supported by jointed ribs, it can open into a fan nearly four meters across or fold tightly against the body. Thousands of overlapping mineral scales cover its surface. They scatter the red sunlight into flashes of rose, amber, and smoky green.

The sail serves several purposes. Opened toward the star, it warms the wanderer’s circulating fluid. Angled into the wind, it provides enough forward pull to help the animal cross the plains with surprisingly little effort. During violent storms, it folds shut, and the wanderer crouches with its hooks sunk into the rock.

The sail also contains living gardens.

In microscopic pockets between the scales grow colonies of dark, light-harvesting organisms. The wanderer supplies them with moisture and mineral waste; in return, they release sugars that seep into its skin. This arrangement does not provide all the energy the animal needs, but it allows it to survive long journeys between feeding grounds.

Those feeding grounds lie along the lakeshores, where leathery mats of microbial life coat the stones. The wanderer lowers its narrow head and unfolds a circular mouth lined with short, comb-like plates. It rasps the mats from the rock, leaving pale spiral marks behind. Two soft feelers beside its mouth taste the surface first. A hungry wanderer may examine a dozen patches before finding one safe to eat.

It has no eyes in the familiar sense. Instead, a band of light-sensitive tissue circles its head, giving it a blurred view in every direction. Fine hairs beneath its belly detect changes in air pressure, while its feet sense vibrations through the ground. A creature approaching from behind may escape its notice in still air, yet be detected immediately by a footfall.

Wanderers usually travel in loose groups of five or six. They communicate by tapping their front legs against stone. Along a continuous slab of bedrock, these rhythms carry farther than their soft, breathy voices. Resting groups often maintain a slow exchange of taps, each animal answering before lowering its head again.

Once every few years, adults gather at warm mineral springs to reproduce. They bury clusters of thumb-sized eggs in damp gravel, then remain nearby for several weeks, scraping channels that keep spring water flowing through the nests.

Newly hatched wanderers have no sails. They are dark, quick little creatures that hide beneath shoreline stones. Their first translucent scales appear only after they acquire the microscopic partners that will inhabit their backs.

Because Nacre’s weak sunlight cannot meet all its energy needs, the glassback also grazes. Its mouth sits beneath its head, sheltered from windblown grit. Two muscular lips peel rubbery mats of native vegetation from rocks, while ridged grinding plates crush them into paste.
